Chest exercise

Push-Up

The push-up is the most accessible upper body strength exercise there is. Done with good form, it trains the chest, shoulders, triceps and core together and can be scaled for almost anyone.

By Khushi Gupta · Reviewed October 2026

Primary
Chest
Also works
Triceps, Front delts, Core, Serratus anterior
Equipment
None (bodyweight)
Level
Beginner

How to do it

  1. Place your hands on the floor slightly wider than shoulder width, fingers pointing forward.
  2. Step your feet back so your body forms a straight line from head to heels. Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs.
  3. Lower your chest toward the floor by bending your elbows, keeping them at about 45 degrees from your body.
  4. Go down until your chest is a fist's width from the floor.
  5. Push the floor away to straighten your arms, keeping your body in one rigid line.
  6. At the top, push slightly further so your shoulder blades spread apart, then start the next rep.

Coaching cues

  • Body like a plank
  • Elbows at 45 degrees, not flared
  • Chest leads, hips follow
  • Push the floor away
Advertisements

Common mistakes and fixes

Sagging hips

Squeeze your glutes and brace your abs. If you still sag, elevate your hands on a bench.

Elbows flared straight out to the sides

Tuck them so your arms form an arrow shape with your body, not a T.

Tiny range of motion

Lower until your chest nearly touches the floor. Use an easier variation if you cannot reach full depth.

Head dropping forward

Keep your neck neutral and look at the floor slightly ahead of your hands.

Sets and reps

GoalPrescription
Strength4-5 sets of 5-10 reps of a hard variation
Hypertrophy3-4 sets of 10-25 reps, stopping 1-3 reps short of failure
Beginner3 sets of 5-10 incline or knee push-ups

Pick a starting weight with the one rep max calculator, and load the bar with the plate calculator.

Variations

  • Incline push-up Hands on a bench or wall to make it easier.
  • Knee push-up A shorter lever for building toward full reps.
  • Decline push-up Feet raised to emphasise the upper chest and shoulders.
  • Diamond push-up Hands close together for more triceps.
  • Deficit or weighted push-up Hands on blocks or a plate on your back to keep progressing.

Muscles worked

Like the bench press, the push-up is driven by the pectoralis major, front delts and triceps.

Unlike the bench, your shoulder blades are free to move, so the serratus anterior works too, and holding a rigid plank turns it into a core exercise.

Benefits

Push-ups need no equipment, so they fit into home workouts, travel days and warm-ups. Studies comparing push-ups and bench presses at similar effort have found similar muscle gains, so they are far more than a warm-up exercise.

They are also a simple fitness test. Tracking how many clean reps you can do is an easy way to see progress.

Safety and who should modify it

If your wrists hurt, use push-up handles or dumbbells to keep your wrists straight, or do them on your fists. Shoulder pain often improves when you tuck your elbows more.

Frequently asked questions

How many push-ups should I do a day?

There is no magic number. Two or three hard sets a few times a week is more effective than hundreds of sloppy reps every day.

Do push-ups build muscle?

Yes, especially for beginners and when taken close to failure. As you get stronger, harder variations or added weight keep them challenging.

Are knee push-ups worth doing?

Yes. They train the same muscles with less load and are a good bridge to full push-ups. Keep your body straight from knees to head.
